nghe.t: Part 1. You will hear a woman telephoning a college to ask about evening courses. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10.
Good afternoon, Northfield College, evening courses. Tom speaking.
Hi. I'm calling to ask about your evening courses this fall. I've seen three on your website that I like, but I have some questions.
Of course. Which courses are you interested in?
First, photography. Is that on Tuesday evenings?
That's right. Tuesdays, from seven to nine.
And the website says it costs £95 for the term.
Ah, I'm afraid that's last year's price. This year it's £105.
£105. OK. Do I need to bring anything? A laptop, for example?
No, we have computers in the classroom. But you do need to bring your own camera. The college doesn't have any for students to borrow.
That's fine. I have a good camera. Now, the second one is Italian for beginners. That's on Mondays, isn't it?
It was on Mondays last term. But the teacher has changed, so this term it's on Wednesdays, from half past six to half past eight.
Wednesdays. Hmm. And the price?
£110. And you will have to buy the course book. Some students ask about a dictionary, but you really don't need one at this level.
OK, just the book. And the last one is the cooking course, on Thursdays.

Yes, World Cooking. That's £150, which sounds a lot, but it includes all the food. It's very popular, and the numbers are limited. The kitchen has space for sixteen people, but the teacher only takes twelve students, so that she can help everybody.
Twelve. I see. Well, I think the cooking course is too expensive for me anyway. I'd like to sign up for photography, please.
Lovely. Let me take your details. What's your name?
Carla Jensen. That's J, E, N, S, E, N.
J, E, N, S, E, N. And your address?
14 Mill Road.
Sorry, was that Hill Road?
No, Mill, with an M. M, I, double L.
Mill Road. Thank you. Now, the term begins on Monday the 14th of September, but as your class is on a Tuesday, your first lesson will be on the 15th.
The 15th of September. Great. How do I pay? Can I bring cash on the first evening?
I'm afraid we don't take cash any more. You can pay online by bank transfer, or by card over the phone.
Then I'll pay by card now, if that's OK.
Perfect. One last question, for our records. How did you hear about the college? Was it our advertisement in the newspaper?
No, I didn't see that. Actually, my neighbour told me about it. She did a painting course with you last year and loved it.
Oh, that's nice to hear. Right, I'll just take your card details.

nhom.huongDan: Part 2 — Câu 11–20. Helen, hướng dẫn viên, nói về kế hoạch buổi đi bộ tham quan phố cổ Wexley rồi giới thiệu 5 điểm sẽ ghé. Cả part là MỘT bài nghe liền, chỉ nghe MỘT lần — bấm nghe rồi lướt qua các câu của part trong lúc nghe.

nghe.t: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of tourists at the start of a walking tour of an old city. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 20.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Wexley. My name is Helen, and I am your guide for today's walking tour of the old city. Before we set off, let me tell you about the plan for the day.

The tour usually lasts three hours. Today, however, the cathedral tower is closed for repairs, so we will not be climbing it, and the tour will take two and a half hours. We will finish back here in the market square at about half past twelve.

Now, the weather. The forecast said rain this morning, but as you can see, the sun has come out, so you will not need your umbrellas. It is warm too, so you can leave your coats on the coach. What you will need is comfortable shoes. Many of the streets in the old city are made of stone, and they are quite hard to walk on.

At about eleven o'clock, we will stop for a break. On most of my tours, we go to a café by the river. But today is Saturday, and on Saturdays there is a wonderful food market in the Corn Hall. So that is where we will have our break. You can try the local cheese and bread there. There is also a tea room in the castle, but it is rather expensive.

A word about photographs. You may take pictures everywhere in the streets, in the castle, and inside the cathedral too, as long as you do not use a flash. The only place where photography is not allowed is the art gallery. Please keep your cameras in your bags there.

And if you get lost, don't worry. Please don't try to phone me, because my phone often has no signal in the old streets. Don't go back to the coach, either, because the driver will not be there. Just come back to the clock tower here in the market square and wait. I will come and find you.

Now, let me tell you about some of the places we are going to see. We will begin with the cathedral. Many visitors believe that it is the oldest building in Wexley, but that isn't true. What makes it interesting is its roof. In 1829, a terrible fire destroyed the roof and most of the windows, and it took thirty years to repair the building.

From the cathedral, we will walk up the hill to the castle. I have to say, there isn't much left inside it, and you do have to pay five pounds to go in. But it is worth it. From the top of the castle walls, you get the best view of the city, and on a clear day like today you can see all the way to the sea.

After that, we go down to the river and the old bridge. It doesn't look very special, but it was built almost nine hundred years ago, a century before the cathedral. Nothing else in the city is as old as that.

Next to the bridge is the city museum. It is quite small, and I have heard that they are planning to build a new section next year. One good thing is that it doesn't cost anything to go in, so do have a look if you have time after the tour.

And our last stop is Weavers' Lane, a narrow street of tiny shops. People often say that it looks like a street in a film, although as far as I know nobody has ever made a film there. The shops sell things that are made locally, such as pottery and woollen scarves. If you want to take presents home for your family, this is the place to get them.
Right. Is everybody ready? Then let's go.

nghe.t: Part 3. You will hear a student radio presenter called Mark interviewing Priya, a journalism student, about her work placement at a local newspaper. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30.

Hello, and welcome to Campus Radio. I'm Mark, and my guest today is Priya, a second-year journalism student who has just finished a three-month work placement at a local newspaper, the Dunmore Gazette. Welcome, Priya.
Thanks, Mark.
So, why did you choose the Gazette? Was it your first choice?

Not really. First I wrote to a television company, but they never replied. Then my tutor recommended a magazine in London, but I couldn't afford to rent a room there. The Gazette's office is ten minutes from my parents' house, so I could live at home for three months. That's what decided it.
Very sensible. And what was your first week like? Were you writing news stories from day one?
I wish! I thought I would be out interviewing people. In fact, for the whole of the first week, I sat at a desk and read other reporters' articles, looking for spelling mistakes.
That sounds a bit boring.
It was, but I learned a lot about how news stories are written.
What was the most difficult thing about the job?

Before I started, I was worried about telephoning strangers. But after a couple of days, that was fine. And I didn't mind the early mornings, even though we started at eight. No, the hardest thing was writing fast. At university, we have a week to write an article. At the Gazette, I sometimes had one hour.
Wow. And what about your boss, the editor? I've heard that editors can be quite frightening.

People told me that he was unfriendly, and he does look very serious. But he always found time to read my work, and he told me exactly what was wrong with it and how to make it better. I've never had such helpful advice.
So which skills did you improve most?

Well, not photography. The Gazette has its own photographer, so I never touched a camera. And I worked alone most of the time, so I can't say I learned much about teamwork. But I'm much better at writing headlines now. A good headline has to be short and clear, and that's harder than it sounds.
Anything else?
Yes, checking facts. Every name, every date, every number has to be checked twice. I used to be quite careless about that. I'm not any more.
Now, tell our listeners how a story actually gets into the newspaper. What happens during the day?
OK. The day starts at eight o'clock with a meeting. The editor and all the reporters sit down together and choose the stories for that day's paper.
And then you go out and find people to talk to?
That's what I imagined. But actually, most interviews are done by phone, because it's so much quicker. Reporters only go out for the really big stories.
I see. And when the story is written?

It goes to the editor. He reads it, and he nearly always makes it shorter, because there is never enough space on the page. After that, a photograph is added, and someone checks the whole page one last time.
And when does the paper have to be finished?
At four o'clock, the finished pages are sent to the printer. By six, the Gazette is in the shops.
Fascinating. Priya, thank you very much.

nghe.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about the tides. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

Good morning, everyone. Today, we are going to look at something that anybody who has spent a day at the beach has noticed: the tides. Twice a day, the sea rises up the beach, and twice a day it goes back down again. I am going to explain why this happens, why some tides are bigger than others, and how tides affect people.

Let's begin with the cause. People in ancient times already knew that the tides were connected with the Moon, but they did not know why. The first person who explained it correctly was Isaac Newton, in 1687. The explanation is gravity. The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth, and because water can move easily, the water in the oceans is pulled towards the Moon. This creates a kind of hill of water on the side of the Earth that faces the Moon and, for reasons that I will not go into today, a second hill on the opposite side.

Now, the Earth is turning all the time. As it turns, each coast passes through both of these hills of water. That is why most places have two high tides and two low tides each day. But here is a detail that surprises many people. The time between one high tide and the next is not exactly twelve hours. It is about twelve hours and twenty-five minutes. So the tides arrive nearly an hour later each day.
The Sun also pulls on the oceans. The Sun is much bigger than the Moon, of course, but it is very much further away, so its effect on the tides is less than half as strong.

When the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are in a straight line, the Sun and the Moon pull together. This happens at the time of a new moon and a full moon, and it gives us especially large tides. We call them spring tides. Be careful: the name has nothing to do with the season. It comes from an old word that means "to jump". About a week later, the Sun and the Moon are pulling in different directions, and the tides are small. These are called neap tides. I will spell that for you: N, E, A, P.

The size of the tide also depends on the shape of the coast. In most of the Mediterranean Sea, the difference between high tide and low tide is less than half a metre. But in the Bay of Fundy, on the east coast of Canada, the water can rise by sixteen metres. That is the height of a five-storey building. Those are the highest tides in the world.

So why do tides matter? First, for ships. Large ships can only enter some ports at high tide, when the water is deep enough. For this reason, tide tables, which give the times of the tides, are published a year or more in advance. Second, tides can be dangerous. Every year, visitors walking on wide beaches are surprised by how quickly the sea comes in, and they find themselves cut off from the land.

And finally, tides can give us energy. As the water flows in and out, it can turn machines that produce electricity. The first large power station of this kind was opened in 1966 in the north-west of France, and it is still working today. Unlike the wind, the tides are completely reliable: we know exactly when they will come. The main disadvantage is cost. Building the stations is extremely expensive. We will talk more about ocean energy next week.

READING PASSAGE 1
A WHEEL FOR A NEW CENTURY
The London Eye was planned as a temporary attraction. A quarter of a century later, it is still turning

Every year, more than three million people queue on the south bank of the River Thames to take a slow ride into the sky. The London Eye, a giant observation wheel 135 metres high, has become one of the best-known sights in Britain. On a clear day, passengers at the top can see for about 40 kilometres. Yet when it was first suggested, many people thought that it would never be built – and it was only meant to stand for five years.
The story began in 1993, when a newspaper and an architecture organisation held a competition. They asked for designs for a new landmark to celebrate the year 2000. Two London architects, David Marks and Julia Barfield, who were husband and wife, sent in their idea for a great wheel beside the river. The judges, however, were not satisfied with any of the designs, and no winner was chosen. Marks and Barfield refused to give up. They believed in their wheel so strongly that they borrowed money against their own home, and they spent the next few years looking for investors and for a place to put it.
The design was unusual. Most big wheels, such as those at fairs, are held up on both sides. The London Eye, which is 120 metres across, is supported on one side only, by a huge A-shaped frame that leans towards the water. This means that nothing stands between the passengers and the river. At the centre of the wheel is the hub. Steel cables run from the hub to the rim, the outer circle of the wheel, just like the thin wires in a bicycle wheel. The passengers ride in 32 glass capsules. On older wheels, the cabins hang inside the structure, which blocks part of the view. Here, the capsules are fixed to the outside of the rim, so passengers can see in every direction.
Building the wheel was an international project. The steel came from Britain and was cut and shaped in the Netherlands. The cables were made in Italy, the hub was made in the Czech Republic, and the capsules were built in France. The parts of the wheel were carried up the Thames on boats and put together lying flat, on platforms in the river. Then the wheel was slowly lifted, at about two degrees an hour, until it reached an angle of 65 degrees. It stayed in that position for a week while engineers prepared the second stage of the lift.
The Prime Minister officially opened the London Eye on 31 December 1999, but there were no passengers that night. A technical problem with the capsules had been found, and the public had to wait until March 2000 for their first ride. Since then, the wheel has hardly stopped. It turns so slowly – at less than one kilometre an hour, so that one full circle takes about half an hour – that people can simply walk on and off while it is moving. It only stops when disabled or elderly passengers need extra time. Each capsule holds up to 25 people, who are free to walk around inside. The capsules are numbered from 1 to 33; because some people believe that 13 is unlucky, there is no capsule with that number. In one hour, about 1,600 people can take the ride.
When it opened, the London Eye was the tallest observation wheel in the world. It lost that title in 2006 to a wheel in China, and taller ones have been built since. For a few more years, it remained the highest public viewing point in London, until a platform opened near the top of a new skyscraper, the Shard, in 2013. But height is not the reason for its success. The local council had at first given permission for only five years. The wheel was so popular, however, that in 2002 the council agreed that it could stay permanently. Today it appears in films, on postcards and in countless holiday photographs of London. A structure that the competition judges did not want has become one of the symbols of the city.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 2
THE LONG ROAD OF THE MARATHON
How a legend from ancient Greece became a race for everyone

A  Every year, more than 800 marathons are held around the world, and huge numbers of ordinary people run a distance that was once thought to be dangerous even for trained athletes. The race is named after a place in Greece, and its story begins – if the legend is true – with a single runner. In 490 BC, the army of Athens defeated a Persian army near the village of Marathon. According to the legend, a messenger ran all the way to Athens with the news. He cried, "We have won!" and then fell down dead.
B  For more than two thousand years, nobody thought of turning this story into a sport. Then, in the 1890s, plans were made for the first modern Olympic Games, which were held in Athens in 1896. A French professor, Michel Bréal, suggested a race from Marathon to the Olympic stadium, a distance of about 40 kilometres, and he offered a silver cup to the winner. Seventeen runners started. The Greek public badly wanted a Greek to win, and they were not disappointed. The race was won by Spyridon Louis, a young man who earned his living by carrying water. When he entered the stadium, two Greek princes ran beside him to the finishing line. He finished in just under three hours and became a national hero.
C  The first Olympic marathons were all about 40 kilometres long, but the exact distance changed from one Games to the next. Conditions could be terrible: at the Games of 1904 in St Louis, the runners had to compete on dusty roads in great heat, and fewer than half of them finished. The length that runners know today – 42.195 kilometres – comes from the London Olympics of 1908. The organisers planned a route of 26 miles from Windsor Castle to the stadium. They then added part of a lap of the track, 385 yards, so that the race would end in front of the seats of the royal family. In 1921, this strange figure was fixed as the official distance for all marathons.
D  For most of the twentieth century, the marathon was for men only. Officials claimed that women's bodies were too weak for such a long race. Women runners knew better. In 1966, an American, Bobbi Gibb, waited behind a bush near the start of the famous Boston Marathon, joined the runners and finished ahead of most of the men. The next year, Kathrine Switzer entered the same race. On the entry form she wrote only her initials, "K. V. Switzer", so the organisers did not realise that she was a woman, and she was given an official number. During the race, an angry official ran after her and tried to pull the number off her shirt, but she got away and reached the finish. Photographs of the moment appeared in newspapers around the world.

READING PASSAGE 3
WHY SLOW NEWS MATTERS
A journalist argues that getting the news faster has not made us wiser

A hundred years ago, news arrived once a day, when the morning newspaper landed on the doorstep. Fifty years ago, most families also watched the evening news on television. People had time to think about what they had read or heard before the next news arrived. Today, news never stops. It reaches us through our phones at every hour of the day and night, often before reporters have had time to check what really happened. Many people believe that this makes us the best-informed generation in history. I think they are mistaken.
It is true that we see more news than ever before. But seeing is not the same as understanding. In my view, a person who reads twenty short headlines on a phone often knows less at the end of the day than someone who has read one long article carefully. A headline tells us that something has happened. It rarely tells us why it happened, or what is likely to happen next. Yet surveys suggest that most of us now read little more than the headline before we move on to the next story. The same is true of the short videos that many young people now use as their main source of news: they are easy to watch, but thirty seconds is not long enough to explain a war or an election.
The speed of modern news creates a second problem: mistakes. When a big story breaks, every news website wants to be first, and being first has become more important than being right. Early reports of an accident or a storm are frequently wrong about the most basic facts, such as the number of people who were hurt. The mistakes are usually corrected a few hours later. Unfortunately, by then the first version has been shared thousands of times, and few people ever see the correction. I have seen this happen many times in my own work as a journalist.
News companies are not entirely to blame for this situation. Journalists are not bad people; the problem is the way in which the business now works. Most of them no longer earn much money from selling newspapers. Instead, they depend on advertising, and advertisers pay according to the number of people who click on a story. As a result, editors choose the stories that will attract the most clicks, and these are usually stories that make readers angry or afraid. Good news, and slow changes that take years, receive very little attention. Readers are therefore left with the feeling that the world is more dangerous than it actually is.
There is also a cost to our health. A psychologist whom I interviewed for this article, Dr Hannah Reeve, asked two hundred adults to switch off all the news alerts on their phones for one month. They were still allowed to read or watch the news once a day, at a time that they chose. At the end of the month, most of them reported that they felt calmer and slept better. More surprisingly, when they were given a short test on recent events, they did just as well as people who had kept their alerts on. In other words, the alerts had been adding stress without adding knowledge. Dr Reeve told me that she had expected the opposite result.
Some journalists have reacted to these problems by starting what they call "slow news". Instead of publishing hundreds of stories a day, a slow-news organisation may publish only three or four. Its reporters wait until the facts are clear, and then explain the background in detail. One magazine in Britain even prints its stories three months after the events have happened. Such organisations are usually paid for by their readers rather than by advertisers, so they do not need to chase clicks. So far, their audiences are small, and I doubt that slow news will ever replace the fast kind. People will always want to know immediately when something important happens.
Nevertheless, I believe that we can all learn something from the idea. We do not have to give up our phones. We can, however, decide when we read the news, instead of letting the news decide for us. We can choose one or two sources that we trust and ignore the rest. And when a dramatic story appears, we can wait a day before we share it. None of this is difficult, and none of it costs anything. Schools could help too, by teaching children how to judge whether a news story can be trusted. The news will go on getting faster. That does not mean that we have to.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 3
WHY SLOW NEWS MATTERS
A journalist argues that getting the news faster has not made us wiser

A hundred years ago, news arrived once a day, when the morning newspaper landed on the doorstep. Fifty years ago, most families also watched the evening news on television. People had time to think about what they had read or heard before the next news arrived. Today, news never stops. It reaches us through our phones at every hour of the day and night, often before reporters have had time to check what really happened. Many people believe that this makes us the best-informed generation in history. I think they are mistaken.
It is true that we see more news than ever before. But seeing is not the same as understanding. In my view, a person who reads twenty short headlines on a phone often knows less at the end of the day than someone who has read one long article carefully. A headline tells us that something has happened. It rarely tells us why it happened, or what is likely to happen next. Yet surveys suggest that most of us now read little more than the headline before we move on to the next story. The same is true of the short videos that many young people now use as their main source of news: they are easy to watch, but thirty seconds is not long enough to explain a war or an election.
The speed of modern news creates a second problem: mistakes. When a big story breaks, every news website wants to be first, and being first has become more important than being right. Early reports of an accident or a storm are frequently wrong about the most basic facts, such as the number of people who were hurt. The mistakes are usually corrected a few hours later. Unfortunately, by then the first version has been shared thousands of times, and few people ever see the correction. I have seen this happen many times in my own work as a journalist.
News companies are not entirely to blame for this situation. Journalists are not bad people; the problem is the way in which the business now works. Most of them no longer earn much money from selling newspapers. Instead, they depend on advertising, and advertisers pay according to the number of people who click on a story. As a result, editors choose the stories that will attract the most clicks, and these are usually stories that make readers angry or afraid. Good news, and slow changes that take years, receive very little attention. Readers are therefore left with the feeling that the world is more dangerous than it actually is.
There is also a cost to our health. A psychologist whom I interviewed for this article, Dr Hannah Reeve, asked two hundred adults to switch off all the news alerts on their phones for one month. They were still allowed to read or watch the news once a day, at a time that they chose. At the end of the month, most of them reported that they felt calmer and slept better. More surprisingly, when they were given a short test on recent events, they did just as well as people who had kept their alerts on. In other words, the alerts had been adding stress without adding knowledge. Dr Reeve told me that she had expected the opposite result.
Some journalists have reacted to these problems by starting what they call "slow news". Instead of publishing hundreds of stories a day, a slow-news organisation may publish only three or four. Its reporters wait until the facts are clear, and then explain the background in detail. One magazine in Britain even prints its stories three months after the events have happened. Such organisations are usually paid for by their readers rather than by advertisers, so they do not need to chase clicks. So far, their audiences are small, and I doubt that slow news will ever replace the fast kind. People will always want to know immediately when something important happens.
Nevertheless, I believe that we can all learn something from the idea. We do not have to give up our phones. We can, however, decide when we read the news, instead of letting the news decide for us. We can choose one or two sources that we trust and ignore the rest. And when a dramatic story appears, we can wait a day before we share it. None of this is difficult, and none of it costs anything. Schools could help too, by teaching children how to judge whether a news story can be trusted. The news will go on getting faster. That does not mean that we have to.
